texts.title: My morning routine
texts.text: I usually wake up at seven o’clock. First, I drink a big glass of water and open the window. Then I take a shower and get dressed. I always have breakfast at home: bread, butter and a cup of coffee. At eight, I leave my flat and walk to the station. The train is often full, so I listen to music or a podcast. I arrive at work at nine. Before I start, I check my emails and say hello to my colleagues. I like my mornings because they are calm and simple.

texts.title: Working from home
texts.text: Since the pandemic, many people work from home two or three days a week. For a lot of employees, it saves time and money, because they do not need to commute. They can also concentrate better without the noise of an open space. However, working from home is not perfect. Some people feel lonely, and it can be difficult to separate work from private life. Managers also worry that teams communicate less. That is why many companies now prefer a hybrid model. Employees come to the office for meetings and team activities, and they stay at home for tasks that need focus.

texts.title: Preparing for a job interview
texts.text: A good job interview starts long before you enter the room. First, research the company: read its website, recent news and the job description carefully. Then prepare a short story about your career, about two minutes long, that explains who you are and why you want this role. Recruiters often ask about a problem you solved, so choose two or three concrete examples and describe the situation, what you did and the result. Do not forget to prepare questions for them too. Asking about the team, the tools or the first projects shows that you are genuinely interested.

texts.title: What a data engineer actually does
texts.text: People often confuse data engineers with data scientists, but their jobs are quite different. A data scientist builds models and answers business questions. A data engineer makes sure the data needed for those questions is available, reliable and up to date. In practice, that means designing pipelines that collect data from many sources, clean it, and store it in a format that analysts can query. A large part of the job is invisible when everything works: monitoring jobs, handling late or broken files, and keeping costs under control. When a dashboard shows the right number at nine in the morning, it is usually thanks to a data engineer.

texts.title: The real cost of meetings
texts.text: Most professionals would agree that they attend too many meetings, yet calendars keep filling up. Part of the problem is that the cost of a meeting is rarely made explicit. An hour-long call with eight people does not cost one hour; it costs eight, plus the time each participant needs to refocus afterwards. Some companies have responded by introducing meeting-free days or by requiring a written agenda before any invitation is sent. Others encourage asynchronous updates, where people share progress in writing and keep live discussions for genuine decisions. The underlying idea is simple: a meeting should be the most effective way to reach an outcome, not a default habit.

texts.title: Small talk, big impact
texts.text: For many non-native speakers, small talk is harder than a technical presentation. A presentation follows a plan, while a casual chat at the coffee machine can go anywhere. Yet these short conversations matter: they build trust and make teamwork easier. The good news is that small talk follows predictable patterns. People talk about the weekend, the weather, travel plans or a recent event. Asking open questions, such as how someone spent their holiday, and sharing a small detail about yourself is usually enough to keep the conversation going. Nobody expects a brilliant speech, just genuine interest.
